reader.title: Attempted lynching of Jeff Gillenwaters
bases: A mob broke into the Senatobia jail, took out a prisoner charged with murder, shot him repeatedly and left him for dead, intending to hang him (A2, A3); he survived (A3, A9).

A mob of twenty or thirty took Gillenwaters from jail over a murder charge and shot him seven or nine times (A2, A3), but he survived, recovered and escaped (A3, A6), so this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The Richland Beacon and the Memphis Public Ledger independently describe the mob shooting (A2, A3), the Weekly Clarion reports the six arrests (A1), and the governor's reward description lists the bullet scars (A5).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Jeff Gillenwaters took place at Senatobia, Mississippi, in late September or early October 1881, when a mob took Gillenwaters, a prisoner charged with murder, from the town jail, shot him and left him for dead.
Gillenwaters survived, named his assailants, and six young men were jailed for the attempt.
The case drew notice because a grand jury then failed to indict the accused men and Gillenwaters himself broke jail, prompting a reward from the governor.
Gillenwaters, about 20 years old, was held in the Senatobia jail on a charge of murder.
According to the Richland Beacon, he was charged with the murder of J. T. Eason at Arkabutla, a settlement several miles from Senatobia.
The Memphis Public Ledger instead described the case as the supposed killing of a young store keeper in Tunica county with whom he had been sleeping.
None of the reports states Gillenwaters's race.
On a Saturday morning, a mob of twenty or thirty men broke into the jail, took Gillenwaters out and carried him about a mile and a half from town.
There they shot him, seven times by the Beacon's count and nine by the Ledger's, and left him at the roadside for dead.
The Ledger added that one of the mob rode over the man's body as it lay on the ground and fired into his breast.
The Beacon wrote that the men had meant to hang him, but citizens of Senatobia rang the bells and raised a rescuing party whose pursuit frightened the lynchers off.
It said the lynchers came from Arkabutla, the scene of Eason's murder, and that the townspeople had no part in the act.
Gillenwaters recognized several of his attackers and, in what was taken for a dying statement, gave their names to the authorities.
By 6 October six young men charged with attempting to lynch him had been captured and jailed without bond, and Gen. J. R. Chalmers was to defend them.
Meanwhile Gillenwaters recovered from his wounds.
On the night of 19 October 1881, Gillenwaters, by then under indictment for murder, broke jail at Senatobia.
The Ledger reported a hint that friends of the murdered man had connived at the escape.
The Weekly Panola Star reported that the grand jury failed to indict the men charged with lynching him.
Governor J. M. Stone offered a $250 reward for his arrest, and the notice described bullet scars on his face, back, shoulder, ribs and arm.
Coverage came entirely from white papers, mostly in Mississippi and Memphis.
The Jackson Weekly Clarion and the Panola Star treated the arrests and the escape as one-line items among state news.
The Clarion also ran the governor's proclamation in its 3, 10 and 16 November issues.

The fullest account appeared under the heading "Lynch Law" in the Richland Beacon of Rayville, Louisiana, whose text speaks of "our neighboring town of Senatobia" and so appears to reprint a nearby Mississippi paper.
It demanded "strict and stern justice" for the "masked night-riders" and declared that "Lynch law is no law at all," while still calling the prisoner "wretched" and the murder "brutal and cowardly."
The Public Ledger headed its item "Has Gone Free" and dwelt on Gillenwaters's "nine bullet holes."
As late as 17 November, a West Virginia paper reported that the lynchers were "in trouble" and promised a vigorous prosecution.
The accounts differ on the number of shots, seven in the Beacon and nine in the Ledger.

They also differ on the alleged murder: the Beacon names J. T. Eason at Arkabutla, while the Ledger describes a young Tunica county store keeper and places the dying statement with Tunica authorities.
The Beacon's version comes from near Senatobia, and the governor's notice places the case in Tate county.

accounts.label: Senatobia-area account (Richland Beacon)
accounts.gist: A mob of twenty or thirty from Arkabutla took Gillenwaters from jail, shot him seven times a mile and a half from town and left him for dead; townspeople's pursuit kept them from hanging him, and six men he recognized were jailed.

accounts.label: Memphis report
accounts.gist: Gillenwaters, held over the supposed killing of a young Tunica county store keeper, had been shot nine times and left at the roadside; his dying statement named six men; after recovering he escaped, with a hint that friends of the murdered man connived.

accounts.label: Governor's proclamation
accounts.gist: Gillenwaters, under indictment for murder, broke jail at Senatobia on the night of 19 October 1881; $250 reward offered.

framing.detail: Under 'Lynch Law' the Beacon called for 'strict and stern justice' for the 'masked night-riders' and declared 'Lynch law is no law at all', while calling the prisoner 'wretched' and the murder 'brutal and cowardly'.
The Memphis Public Ledger headed its escape item 'Has Gone Free', dwelt on the nine bullet holes and hinted at connivance by friends of the murdered man.
Mississippi papers carried one-line state-news items on the arrests and the escape, and the Clarion printed the governor's reward notice.
